2023_071_creating_a_culture_of_connected.paragraph: An Association for Middle Level Education (AMLE) article, "Creating a Culture of Connectedness through Middle School Advisory Programs" by Sarah Brody Shulkind and Jack Foote, printed from amle.org on 3/3/23 and included with Troy School District Board of Education materials for the March 7, 2023 meeting. Drawing on questionnaires, advisor interviews, observations, and student focus groups at three diverse middle schools with successful advisory programs, the authors identify seven characteristics of advisors and advisories that foster connectedness. The most striking reported finding is that 98% of focus-group students answered affirmatively when asked whether advisory helps them academically. The piece was previously published in Middle School Journal, September 2009.
2023_071_creating_a_culture_of_connected.page:
**Item**
Browser printout of the AMLE (Association for Middle Level Education) web article "Creating a Culture of Connectedness through Middle School Advisory Programs," captured 3/3/23 at 2:24 PM from https://www.amle.org/creating-a-culture-of-connectedness-through-middle-school-advisory-programs/, pages 1/7 through 6/7. Byline: Sarah Brody Shulkind, Jack Foote (Rick Wormeli also appears in the adjacent page furniture). Filed as Troy School District Board of Education material dated March 7, 2023. Closing note: "Previously published in Middle School Journal, September 2009."

**Premise**
Four Los Angeles middle school students answer the question "Does advisory help you feel connected to school?" A seventh grade girl says that without advisory "school would be more distant"; an eighth grade boy describes a bond in which "from 6th sixth grade to 12th grade, everyone shares that connection with one teacher"; a seventh grade boy calls advisory "a place where you can get stuff off your chest."

**Definitions**
Connectedness is defined as a school culture in which students have meaningful relationships with adults in the school, are engaged in the school, and feel a sense of belonging. The authors state it is linked to higher grades, higher test scores, and lower dropout rates regardless of socioeconomic status, citing Blum & Libbey (2004), Jackson & Davis (2000), Klem & Connell (2004), Mac Iver & Epstein (1991), McNeely & Falci (2004), and the National Association of Secondary School Principals (2006). Advisory programs are configurations in which an adult advisor meets regularly during the school day with a group of students for academic and social-emotional mentorship, personalization, and a small peer community of learners.

**Method**
Every advisor and student at three diverse middle schools with successful advisory programs received a questionnaire designed to establish which advisories fostered high levels of connectedness. The three advisories with the highest connectedness at each site were selected; researchers interviewed the advisors, observed the advisories, and ran focus groups with advisees. Seven characteristics emerged at all three sites.

**Figure 1 - Advisor/advisory characteristics that foster connectedness**

| Characteristic |
| --- |
| Strong advisory programs address issues of community. |
| Strong advisories promote open communication. |
| Strong advisors know and care about their advisees. |
| Strong advisors closely supervise their advisees' academic progress. |
| Strong advisors are problem solvers and advice givers. |
| Students and advisors perceive that advisory directly improves academic performance. |
| Students and advisors perceive that advisory functions as a community of learners. |

**Findings**
Community: advisors used family language ("we are a family"); one school used a conversation protocol for positive feedback and behavior issues; another paired seventh graders with eighth grade buddies, called "a pay it forward thing." Observed students were not self-segregated ethnically and refrained from teasing.
Communication: trust walks, team-building games, spotlight activities, a blindfolded obstacle course, and Monday morning circles. In more than half of the advisories observed, students shared emotions publicly.
Academic monitoring: advisors consulted other teachers, used official quarter and semester progress reports, and posted checklists during weekly advisory work time. Asked whether advisors notice struggles, one student said, "Immediately, they are all on it."
Perceived academic effect: 98% of focus-group students said advisory helps them academically. Advisors agreed but split on immediacy - "right away" versus "in the long run."
Community of learners: peer tutoring and study groups formed during guided work time, with one advisor describing a "slip streaming effect." In one observed advisory the advisor asked, "Who can help Damion with this question?" prompting a debate among five students.

**Authors**
Sarah Brody Shulkind, middle school principal, Milken Community High School, Los Angeles, CA (sshulkind@milkenschool.org). Jack Foote, principal, Joseph Le Conte Middle School, Los Angeles, CA (jackfoote@gmail.com).
2023_071_creating_a_culture_of_connected.verbose:
**Source and provenance**
Filed with Troy School District (Michigan) Board of Education materials dated March 7, 2023, the item is a browser printout of an Association for Middle Level Education (AMLE) article at https://www.amle.org/creating-a-culture-of-connectedness-through-middle-school-advisory-programs/, timestamped 3/3/23, 2:24 PM and paginated 1/7 through 6/7. Title: "Creating a Culture of Connectedness through Middle School Advisory Programs." Byline: "By: Sarah Brody Shulkind, Jack Foote," with the name Rick Wormeli in the adjacent page furniture. Captured site navigation includes Search, Join, Renew, Login; an "Explore These Topics" list (COVID-19, Literacy, Math, Reading, Student Engagement, Teacher Motivation, Writing, Social Emotional Learning, Student Motivation); a "Categories / Select Category" selector; and a "Most Popular" list ("Schools of Distinction," "Kindness is harder than it looks," "AMLE Celebrates Inaugural," "Reimagining School - What should it look like and who is it for?"). A closing line reads "Previously published in Middle School Journal, September 2009."

**Opening student voices**
In "an ordinary Los Angeles school," four middle school students answer "Does advisory help you feel connected to school?" A seventh grade girl: "Without advisory school would be more distant. It would not be as cheerful." An eighth grade boy: "from 6th sixth grade to 12th grade, everyone shares that connection with one teacher... it is a place where teachers really know you and understand you." An eighth grade girl: "at least there is always one so you are not nervous about going to school." A seventh grade boy names sixth grade as when "you have violence problems or drug problems or even academic problems or personal problems," and calls advisory "a place where you can get stuff off your chest."

**Connectedness and supporting literature**
Connectedness is defined as a characteristic of school cultures in which students have meaningful relationships with adults within the school, are engaged in the school, and feel a sense of belonging to the school. The authors assert it is linked to higher grades, higher test scores, and lower dropout rates regardless of students' socioeconomic status, citing Blum & Libbey, 2004; Jackson & Davis, 2000; Klem & Connell, 2004; Mac Iver & Epstein, 1991; McNeely & Falci, 2004; and National Association of Secondary School Principals, 2006. Schools organized to promote personalization and communities of learners better prepare adolescents for later success as adults (Carnegie Council on Adolescent Development, 1989), and improving connectedness is urgent at the middle level "because the roots of alienation take hold during early adolescence."

**Advisory defined; the evidence gap**
Advisory programs are broadly defined as configurations in which an adult advisor meets regularly during the school day with a group of students to provide academic and social-emotional mentorship and support, to create personalization within the school, and to facilitate a small peer community of learners (Cushman, 1990; Galassi et al., 2004; Galassi et al., 1997; Juvonen et al., 2004; National Association of Secondary School Principals, 2006; Stevenson, 1998). Although promoted in the literature and intuitively valued by practitioners, advisory has had limited empirical support and no accepted basis for identifying best practices, leaving schools to rely on intuition and anecdote when building programs and training advisors.

**Methodology**
Every advisor and student at three diverse middle schools with successful advisory programs completed a questionnaire designed to establish which advisories fostered high levels of connectedness, identifying which students felt most connected, which advisories reported high connectedness, and which advisors perceived the same levels as their advisees. The three advisories with the highest connectedness at each site were selected; the researchers interviewed those advisors, observed the advisories, and conducted focus groups with the advisees. Seven salient characteristics emerged at all three sites (Figure 1).

**Figure 1 - Advisor/advisory characteristics that foster connectedness**

| Characteristic |
| --- |
| Strong advisory programs address issues of community. |
| Strong advisories promote open communication. |
| Strong advisors know and care about their advisees. |
| Strong advisors closely supervise their advisees' academic progress. |
| Strong advisors are problem solvers and advice givers. |
| Students and advisors perceive that advisory directly improves academic performance. |
| Students and advisors perceive that advisory functions as a community of learners. |

**Community**
High-connectedness advisories worked on how students related to one another. One advisor: "I like to stress that we are a family. So, we do not laugh at each other and nobody makes comments... I am trying to break them of snickering." Another discussed friendship and ostracism; a third handled conflict by telling students, "This is like our little family away from home." One school used a conversation protocol for positive feedback that asked students to "address issues that are caused by the behavior of someone in advisory." Another advisor asked advisees to be "big brother or sister" to a struggling classmate. Two comments recurred in every focus group: advisory is a family, and advisory helps students bond. During observations students were not self-segregated ethnically and refrained from teasing and put-downs. Cross-grade work included addressing sixth graders' problems with older students at one school and assigning seventh graders an eighth grade buddy at another - "kind of like a pay it forward thing."

**Open communication**
Advisors described spotlight get-to-know-you activities, trust walks, and team-building games; at one school Monday mornings began with a circle where students shared what was on their minds. One advisor set up a blindfolded obstacle course: "The rest of you are going to have to listen and trust the person that is verbalizing to you." Students called the communication "intense" and said "people are really vulnerable, and we all share our feelings." In more than half of the advisories observed, students shared emotions publicly; in one, a conversation about crying followed an advisor sharing his own feelings, and when a student asked "Are you crying?" the advisees looked on without giggling. Students initiated conversations about parents fighting, disagreements with friends, problems with a teacher, and academic difficulties, and cited lunch and after school as "other good times to talk." Layout pull quotes read "Strong advisors give their advisees individualized attention," "Advisory programs foster meaningful peer relationships," and "Advisory programs strengthen connectedness in middle grades schools."

**Academic supervision**
Students said advisors "know everything" about their academic standing - "Even if she does not know right away, she will find out" - and found that helpful. Advisors talked with other teachers both in reaction to poor work and low grades and proactively when they had not heard about an advisee in a while; almost every advisor cited official progress reports at the end of the quarter and semester. One recounted a boy "amazing in one class and failing another": "You get an A in math and science, and you are failing social studies. How is that possible?" - he saved social studies homework and never got to it. Students at all three sites had time to do work during advisory weekly, and many advisors posted a checklist of tasks on the board, some items for the whole group and some for specific students.

**Problem solving**
Students unanimously said they would go to their advisors for advice on bullying, friendship strife, homework dilemmas, and other middle school "drama." Advisors called problem-solving sessions "organic" and "responsive to the needs of my kids," reporting racial tension, weak grades, misunderstandings with teachers, school policy, bullying and exclusion, and stress at home. They emphasized problem solving with students rather than for them, answering "What should I do about...?" with "How would you solve that problem?" and "What do you think are your next steps?"

**Perceived academic impact**
Survey data at all three schools indicated students and advisors perceived that advisory improved academic performance, and students in high-connectedness advisories were more likely than those in lower-connectedness advisories to perceive that link. In the focus groups, 98% of students responded affirmatively to "Do you think advisory helps you academically?" Students cited focus on studies, critical academic support, strategizing about classes and teachers, goal setting, and belonging to a group of peers striving for success. The advisor survey confirmed the qualitative findings; advisors assigned advisory a significant role in academic success but disagreed on immediacy, some saying "right away" and others "in the long run." One advisor: "create a good climate, and you are going to have kids who perform at a good academic level." Another called advisory "an academic support" because "middle school kids [do not] know how to talk with teachers and advocate for themselves."

**Community of learners**
Students described advisees as an academic resource: "there is a lot of unseen potential when you can have students help one another." Advisors used the language of peer tutoring and study groups; one linked it to connectedness: "They pull out homework and help each other... They feel connected to school and connected to their teacher and curriculum." In observations at one school, desks were clustered in groups of four with students quizzing each other, and another group sat on the floor with their advisor reviewing for a test. At another school, when a boy exclaimed "I do not get this!" a girl explained mathematical functions; two students worked a problem at the board; and an advisor turned a question back to the group - "Are negative numbers real numbers? Who can help Damion with this question?" - producing a debate among five students about the nature of numbers. One advisor described a "slip streaming effect" in which "the group seems to be pulling them along."

**Conclusion**
As students approach adulthood schools often become more isolating and impersonal; advisory is presented as "the one place in school where students are intimately known as a 'whole child,'" with the potential to ensure every child has a meaningful relationship with an adult and belongs to a community of peers.

**Authors**
Sarah Brody Shulkind, middle school principal at Milken Community High School, Los Angeles, CA (sshulkind@milkenschool.org). Jack Foote, principal of Joseph Le Conte Middle School, Los Angeles, CA (jackfoote@gmail.com).

**References**
Blum & Libbey (2004), Journal of School Health, 74(7), 231-235; Carnegie Council on Adolescent Development (1989), Turning points, Carnegie Corporation; Cushman (1990), Horace, 7(1), 5-17; Galassi, Gulledge & Cox (2004), Advisory, National Middle School Association; Galassi, Gulledge & Cox (1997), Review of Educational Research, 67(3), 301-338; Jackson & Davis (2000), Turning points 2000, Teachers College Press; Juvonen, Le, Kaganoff, Augustine & Constant (2004), Focus on the wonder years, RAND Corporation; Klem & Connell (2004), Journal of School Health, 74(7), 262-273; Mac Iver & Epstein (1991), American Journal of Education, 99(4), 587-622; McNeely & Falci (2004), Journal of School Health, 74(7), 284-293; National Association of Secondary School Principals (2006), Breaking ranks in the middle, Reston, VA; Stevenson (1998), Teaching ten to fourteen year olds (2nd ed.), Addison Wesley Longman.
